deck.section_name: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry
deck.title: Characteristic Organic Reactions

front_blocks.md: Define **addition reaction**.

back_blocks.md: An **addition reaction** is an organic reaction in which two or more molecules combine to give a **single product** with no other products formed.

cards.back_md: An **addition reaction** is an organic reaction in which two or more molecules combine to give a **single product** with no other products formed.

front_blocks.md: What is the difference between a substitution reaction and an elimination reaction?

back_blocks.md: A **substitution** reaction replaces one atom or group with another, whereas an **elimination** reaction removes a small molecule (such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl) from an organic molecule to form a new bond.

cards.front_md: What is the difference between a substitution reaction and an elimination reaction?
cards.back_md: A **substitution** reaction replaces one atom or group with another, whereas an **elimination** reaction removes a small molecule (such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl) from an organic molecule to form a new bond.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In organic chemistry, oxidation involves the addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
In organic chemistry, **oxidation** is typically the addition of oxygen or removal of hydrogen atoms. The symbol **[O]** represents one oxygen atom from an oxidising agent.

front_blocks.md: Define **condensation reaction**.

back_blocks.md: A **condensation reaction** is a reaction in which two organic molecules join together and in the process eliminate a small molecule such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl.

cards.back_md: A **condensation reaction** is a reaction in which two organic molecules join together and in the process eliminate a small molecule such as H<sub>2</sub>O or HCl.

front_blocks.md: Saturated hydrocarbons contain **..........**  bonds only, while unsaturated hydrocarbons contain carbon-carbon **..........**  or **..........**  bonds.

back_blocks.md: Saturated hydrocarbons contain **single** bonds only, while unsaturated hydrocarbons contain carbon-carbon **double** or **triple** bonds.

cards.front_md: Saturated hydrocarbons contain **..........**  bonds only, while unsaturated hydrocarbons contain carbon-carbon **..........**  or **..........**  bonds.
cards.back_md: Saturated hydrocarbons contain **single** bonds only, while unsaturated hydrocarbons contain carbon-carbon **double** or **triple** bonds.

front_blocks.md: What is a hydrolysis reaction?

back_blocks.md: A **hydrolysis** reaction is one in which a compound is broken down by **water** (or by dilute acids or alkalis).

cards.back_md: A **hydrolysis** reaction is one in which a compound is broken down by **water** (or by dilute acids or alkalis).

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In organic chemistry, reduction involves the addition of hydrogen or removal of oxygen.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
In organic chemistry, **reduction** is typically the addition of hydrogen atoms or removal of oxygen. The symbol **[H]** represents one hydrogen atom from a reducing agent.

front_blocks.md: A **..........**  reaction replaces an atom or group of atoms with another atom or group, whereas a **..........**  reaction combines two molecules into one with no other products.

back_blocks.md: A **substitution** reaction replaces an atom or group of atoms with another atom or group, whereas an **addition** reaction combines two molecules into one with no other products.

front_blocks.md: In organic redox equations, what do the symbols [O] and [H] represent?

back_blocks.md: **[O]** represents one oxygen atom from an oxidising agent and **[H]** represents one hydrogen atom from a reducing agent. They are used to balance organic redox equations simply.

front_blocks.md: Define **curly arrow (organic mechanisms)**.

back_blocks.md: A **curly arrow** in an organic mechanism represents the movement of an **electron pair**, drawn from the source (a bond or lone pair) to the species that accepts the electrons.

cards.back_md: A **curly arrow** in an organic mechanism represents the movement of an **electron pair**, drawn from the source (a bond or lone pair) to the species that accepts the electrons.

front_blocks.md: What are the three steps of a free-radical substitution reaction, in order?

back_blocks.md: The three steps are **initiation**, **propagation** and **termination**.

cards.front_md: What are the three steps of a free-radical substitution reaction, in order?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In the initiation step of free-radical substitution, UV light breaks the Cl–Cl bond by homolytic fission.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
UV light provides energy to break the **Cl–Cl** bond homolytically, giving each chlorine atom one electron and forming two **chlorine radicals** (Cl<sup>•</sup>).

**True or False?**

cards.back_md:
**True.**

front_blocks.md: Define **electrophilic addition**.

back_blocks.md: An **electrophilic addition** is a reaction in which an electrophile attacks an electron-rich region of a molecule and a small molecule adds across a double bond to give one product.

cards.back_md: An **electrophilic addition** is a reaction in which an electrophile attacks an electron-rich region of a molecule and a small molecule adds across a double bond to give one product.

front_blocks.md: In free-radical substitution propagation, CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → **..........**  + HCl. The alkyl radical then reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> to form **..........**  and regenerate Cl<sup>•</sup>.

back_blocks.md: In free-radical substitution propagation, CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sup>•</sup> → **<sup>•</sup>****CH****<sub>3</sub>** + HCl. The alkyl radical then reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> to form **CH****<sub>3</sub>****Cl** and regenerate Cl<sup>•</sup>.

front_blocks.md: What is nucleophilic substitution and what acts as the leaving group?

back_blocks.md: **Nucleophilic substitution** is a reaction in which an electron-rich nucleophile displaces a halogen atom from a halogenoalkane. The displaced halide ion (X<sup>-</sup>) is the **leaving group**.

cards.back_md: **Nucleophilic substitution** is a reaction in which an electron-rich nucleophile displaces a halogen atom from a halogenoalkane. The displaced halide ion (X<sup>-</sup>) is the **leaving group**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In the termination step of free-radical substitution, only one product is possible.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Multiple products are possible in termination depending on which two radicals combine. For example, <sup>•</sup>CH<sub>3</sub> + <sup>•</sup>CH<sub>3</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> is an **undesirable** by-product.

front_blocks.md: Define **nucleophilic addition**.

back_blocks.md: A **nucleophilic addition** is a reaction in which a nucleophile attacks an electron-deficient region of a molecule, followed by addition of a small molecule to give one product.

cards.back_md: A **nucleophilic addition** is a reaction in which a nucleophile attacks an electron-deficient region of a molecule, followed by addition of a small molecule to give one product.

front_blocks.md: In a halogenoalkane, the C–X carbon is electron-deficient (**..........**) because the halogen is more **..........**  than carbon and pulls electrons towards itself.

back_blocks.md: In a halogenoalkane, the C–X carbon is electron-deficient (**δ+**) because the halogen is more **electronegative** than carbon and pulls electrons towards itself.
